To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the large-eddy simulation method using unstructured grids is capable of simulating unsteady, separated low and high Reynolds-number flows with reasonable accuracy and that the flow about a high Reynolds number sphere at Re D = 1.14×10 6 exhibits a complex, unsteady wake structure dominated by hairpin-like vorticities.

the drag, mean skin-friction and mean pressure distributions of the sphere at a Reynolds numbers of 1.1◊10 4, 1.1 ◊10 5, 1.14 ◊10 6 are in good agreement to experimental results by Ahenbach and Taneda.
the flow around a sphere at Re=1.14◍106 is fully turbulent and the wake is dominated by shedding of large hairpin-like vorgices.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and implementation of a numerical method based on the finite volume method for the solution of incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.
the development of numerical methods for the solution of the Navier-Stokes equations on unstructured grids for complex geometries.
the development of an efficient numerical technique for simulating complex, unsteady, three dimensional flows.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present simulations are in good agreement to the experimental results for the subcritical cases and the supercritical case.
the flow about a smooth sphere at a Reynolds Number of 1.140.106 is fully turbulent and the wake is dominated by shedding of large-scale hairpin vortices.
the present large-eddy simulation model can accurately capture the flow physics and the wake structure of a sphere in a supercritical regime.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present numerical method can be successfully applied to the simulation of high Reynolds number flows with a turbulence model.
the flow about a fixed sphere at a Reynolds of 1.142×106 has been simulated and the wake-flow structure has been analyzed.
we were able to simulate the flow around a sphere using unstructured grids with good agreement with experiments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the large-eddy simulation model can be used to predict flow around a sphere in the supercritical regime.
the unsteady, separated flows around the sphere are very complex and the flow structures change significantly with Reynolds number.
the large-eddy simulation approach can be used successfully in the supercritical regime.
